front: What was the impact of Presidential Reconstruction on African American rights?
p1: Johnson issued mass pardons to Southern whites → Confederate land returned → '40 acres and a mule' never realised.
p2: Black Codes introduced by Southern states → restricted movement, labour, property rights → de facto re-enslavement.
p3: Johnson actively opposed 14th and 15th Amendments → vetoed both → Congress overruled him.

front: What were the key achievements of Radical Reconstruction?
p1: 14th Amendment (1868) → citizenship + equal protection. 15th Amendment (1870) → voting rights for Black men.
p2: Reconstruction Act (1867) → South divided into military districts → Black Codes removed → elections enforced.
p3: 1,500+ African Americans held public office → 22 in Congress → Blanche Bruce: full Senate term for Mississippi.

front: Why did Reconstruction fail?
p1: Hayes–Tilden Compromise (1877) → federal troops withdrawn → 'Redeemer' governments retook the South.
p2: Deaths of Sumner and Stevens + Panic of 1873 → Northern attention shifts → Radical Republican majority diluted.
p3: Slaughterhouse Case (1873) → civil rights ruled a state issue → Supreme Court undermined 14th Amendment.

front: What was the impact of Jim Crow laws on African Americans?
p1: Spread across South from 1877 → segregated schools, transport, hospitals, parks, restaurants, churches.
p2: Voter suppression from 1890 → literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses → Mississippi Black voter registration: 90% (1867) → 6% (1892).
p3: Plessy v Ferguson (1896) → 'separate but equal' constitutional → gave legal cover to all Jim Crow legislation.

front: What was the significance of the Wilmington Coup (1898)?
p1: White supremacists violently overthrew the biracial elected government of Wilmington, North Carolina.
p2: Showed that even legitimate political power could be destroyed by organised white violence without federal protection.
p3: Mississippi v Williams (1898) same year → Supreme Court ruled voter suppression didn't violate 15th Amendment → over 90% disenfranchised by 1900.

front: What was the significance of Booker T. Washington?
p1: Atlanta Compromise (1895) → accepted social segregation in exchange for economic self-improvement → critics saw this as legitimising Jim Crow and abandoning political rights.
p2: Tuskegee Institute (1881) → trained 1,500 Black students in practical skills annually → Negro Business League (1900) → 600 chapters → 50,000+ Black-owned businesses by 1890s → first Black informal presidential advisor (Roosevelt, 1901).
p3: Du Bois argued Washington sacrificed political and social rights for economic gains → founded Niagara Movement (1905) in direct opposition → later NAACP (1909) → exposed limits of accommodation strategy.

front: What were the criticisms of Booker T. Washington's Atlanta Compromise?
p1: Du Bois argued the Atlanta Compromise (1895) sacrificed political and social rights for economic gains — Washington's acceptance of segregation legitimised Jim Crow. Du Bois founded the Niagara Movement (1905) in direct opposition, demanding full civil and political rights.
p2: William Monroe Trotter: Washington's autocratic control of Black organisations ('Tuskegee Machine') — he controlled Black newspapers, charities and political appointments and was suspicious of critics. Ida B. Wells criticised his silence on lynching.
p3: Niagara Movement (1905) → directly led to the NAACP (1909) → Washington's approach was increasingly marginalised after his death (1915). Du Bois's 'talented tenth' theory — education and professional class would lead Black liberation — directly challenged Washington's vocational focus.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the NAACP?
p1: Founded 1909 → Du Bois, Ida B. Wells + white progressives → legal litigation + political pressure strategy.
p2: Key victories: US v Guinn (1915) → grandfather clauses unconstitutional. Smith v Allwright (1944) → all-white primaries banned → Black voter registration 2% (1940) → 12% (1947).
p3: Brown v Board (1954) → Thurgood Marshall proved $43/yr Black vs $179/yr white → 'separate but equal' overturned. Little Rock Nine (1957) organised.

front: What was the significance of Marcus Garvey and UNIA?
p1: Founded UNIA New York branch (1917) → The Negro World newspaper → 200,000 weekly readers. Black Star Line (1919) → 'Back to Africa' movement.
p2: UNIA reached 4 million members by early 1920s → largest Black mass movement in history → Black nationalism + Pan-Africanism.
p3: 'Garvey must go' campaign (1922) after meeting KKK → deported to Jamaica (1927) for mail fraud → federal government action ended movement.

front: What was the role of State Governments in resisting desegregation?
p1: 'State Rights' ideology → argued states should manage affairs without federal interference → used to block civil rights enforcement.
p2: Massive resistance to Brown (1954) → Virginia closed all public schools rather than integrate → 300+ private 'segregation academies' founded.
p3: Wallace: 'segregation today, tomorrow, forever' → stood in University of Alabama doorway 1963. Faubus deployed National Guard against Little Rock Nine (1957).

front: What was the impact of the New Deal on African American political rights?
p1: FDR created informal 'Black Cabinet' → led by Mary McLeod Bethune → influenced New Deal programmes for Black Americans.
p2: Eleanor Roosevelt advocated for civil rights + supported anti-lynching bills. African Americans began voting Democratic in large numbers → major long-term political shift.
p3: Anti-Communist Red Scare → organisations improving AA rights suspected of communism → Du Bois surveilled + harassed → CIO lost funding.

front: What was the significance of the Warren Court (1953–1969)?
p1: Warren Court (1953–69) → considered most liberal Supreme Court in US history → transformed federal protection of civil rights through judicial activism
p2: Brown v Board (1954) → overturned Plessy — 'separate but equal' unconstitutional in education → Brown II (1955): desegregation 'with all deliberate speed' → BUT no firm deadline — 98% of Black Southern students still segregated by 1964
p3: Browder v Gayle (1956) → segregated buses unconstitutional → triggered end of Montgomery Bus Boycott → Boynton v Virginia (1960) → segregation on interstate buses unconstitutional → directly led to Freedom Rides

front: What was the impact of Brown v Board of Education (1954)?
p1: Thurgood Marshall proved Southern states spent $43/yr on Black students vs $179/yr white → Supreme Court overturned 'separate but equal'.
p2: Theoretically impacted 9 million Black children in the South → but no de facto change immediately → by 1964, 98% still attended segregated schools.
p3: Triggered 'massive resistance' across the South → Virginia closed schools → 300+ segregation academies founded → exposed limits of legal victories.

front: What was the strategy and significance of the SCLC?
p1: Founded 1957 → led by Martin Luther King → non-violent direct action → used media + moral pressure to force federal response.
p2: Birmingham Campaign (1963) → Bull Connor's violence vs peaceful protesters → broadcast nationwide → Kennedy announces moral duty to act → Civil Rights Act 1964.
p3: Selma March (1965) → 50% Black population, 1% electorate → Bloody Sunday broadcast nationally → directly led to Voting Rights Act 1965.

front: What was the strategy and significance of SNCC?
p1: Founded 1960 → grassroots, student-led → more radical than SCLC → organised sit-ins, Freedom Rides, voter registration drives.
p2: Selma March (1965) → John Lewis led marchers onto Edmund Pettus Bridge → 'Bloody Sunday' → Voting Rights Act.
p3: 1966 under Stokely Carmichael → rejected non-violence + integration → embraced Black Power → 'Black Power' slogan coined.

front: What was the Albany Campaign (1962) and why did it fail?
p1: SCLC and King targeted Albany, Georgia → Police Chief Laurie Pritchett used non-violent policing → denied King media images of brutality.
p2: No single dramatic confrontation → media lost interest → federal government had no reason to intervene → no legislation resulted.
p3: Key lesson → non-violent direct action only worked when it provoked visible repression on camera → shaped Birmingham Campaign strategy.

front: What were the Greensboro Sit-ins (1960) and why were they significant?
p1: 4 Black students sat at 'white-only' lunch counter in Greensboro, NC → spontaneous non-violent direct action.
p2: Over 70,000 students engaged in sit-ins across the South co-ordinated by SNCC → more than 1,000 businesses desegregated lunch counters.
p3: Demonstrated power of youth-led spontaneous protest → led to founding of SNCC → showed NAACP's legal approach could be complemented by direct action.

front: What were the Freedom Rides (1961) and what did they achieve?
p1: CORE + SNCC → Black and white activists rode interstate buses from Washington D.C. into the Deep South → testing Boynton v Virginia (1960).
p2: Met with violent mobs including fire-bombings in Alabama → national outrage → federal government forced to respond.
p3: Attorney General enforced desegregation of interstate public transport → demonstrated that federal pressure could be forced through confrontation.

front: What was the significance of the Birmingham Campaign (1963)?
p1: King + SCLC targeted Birmingham → Bull Connor used police dogs + fire hoses against peaceful protesters including children → images broadcast worldwide.
p2: Kennedy announced America had a 'moral duty' to intervene → directly led to Civil Rights Act 1964.
p3: Baptist Church bombings (1963) → KKK killed four young girls → no convictions → highlighted state government complicity in racial terror.

front: What was the significance of the March on Washington (1963)?
p1: 250,000 marched for jobs and freedom → King's 'I Have a Dream' speech → largest civil rights demonstration in US history.
p2: Organised by Randolph + Rustin → brought together NAACP, SCLC, SNCC, CORE, NUL → demonstrated broad coalition.
p3: Malcolm X dismissed it as a 'farce' → highlighted divisions between integrationist and nationalist wings of the movement.

front: What was the impact of the Civil Rights Act (1964)?
p1: Removed all Jim Crow segregation across the South → prohibited employment discrimination based on race.
p2: Pushed through by LBJ using 'Johnson treatment' → most significant federal civil rights legislation since Reconstruction.
p3: Limitations → did not address de facto segregation in the North → did not solve economic inequality → enforcement remained weak in many states.

front: What happened during the Selma March and what did it achieve?
p1: Selma: 50% Black population but only 1% of electorate → SCLC + SNCC march to expose voter suppression.
p2: Bloody Sunday → John Lewis led marchers → violent police attack on Edmund Pettus Bridge → broadcast nationwide.
p3: Directly led to Voting Rights Act (1965) → banned all voter suppression → Mississippi Black voter registration: 6% (1964) → 60% (1969).

front: What were the key ideas of Malcolm X and the Nation of Islam?
p1: NOI → Black nationalism + separatism → rejected integration → 'by any means necessary' → self-defence against white supremacy.
p2: NOI grew from 400 members (1952) → 40,000 (1960) under Malcolm X → addressed Northern urban poverty King's movement neglected.
p3: Post-Hajj (1964) → Malcolm X adopted more inclusive vision → broke from NOI → assassinated by NOI members 1965 → became martyr for Black Power.

front: What were the key ideas of Stokely Carmichael and Black Power?
p1: 1966 → took over SNCC → rejected non-violence + integration → coined 'Black Power' slogan during Meredith March.
p2: Black Power = self-determination, Black pride, economic self-sufficiency, community control — not dependence on white liberals.
p3: Alienated white allies + moderate African Americans → CORE lost white funding 1969 → weakened cross-racial coalition that had passed 1964/65 legislation.

front: Why did Black Power rise to prominence in the late 1960s?
p1: Failures of CRM in North → SCLC/NAACP focused on Southern desegregation → Northern urban communities still faced poverty + police violence. King's Chicago (1966) failed.
p2: Vietnam War → African Americans disproportionately drafted → returned radicalised → war severed King–LBJ relationship → media attention shifted.
p3: Long Hot Summers → Watts (1965) $40m damage → 150 riots (1967) → showed non-violence couldn't address systemic Northern inequality.

front: What was the impact of Nixon's and Reagan's policies on African Americans?
p1: Nixon's 'Law and Order' (1968) → War on Drugs → disproportionately targeted Black communities. Reagan (1981–89) → welfare cuts deepened economic disparities → school desegregation reversed through judicial weakening of bussing → by 1992, 40% of Black students in majority-Black schools.
p2: Supreme Court became increasingly conservative under Reagan → affirmative action weakened → Bakke (1978) precedent extended. Reagan and Bush labelled affirmative action 'reverse discrimination' and reduced federal enforcement.
p3: By 1992 → 25% of Black men in prison, on parole or probation → War on Drugs described by Nixon aide John Ehrlichman as deliberately targeting Black communities. 33% of African Americans below poverty line by 1992.

front: What was the political position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: 8,000+ African Americans held public office → Congressional Black Caucus: 36 members → Thurgood Marshall (1967–91) first Black Supreme Court Justice. Douglas Wilder first Black governor (Virginia, 1989).
p2: Voter turnout 54% vs 61% white → unofficial suppression continued → gerrymandering + insufficient polling locations in Black areas.
p3: Jesse Jackson's 1984 + 1988 presidential campaigns won 7 million votes → but never official Democrat candidate → no Black presidential or VP candidate in the period.

front: What was the impact of the Freedmen's Bureau?
p1: Established 1865 → helped create 1,000+ Black schools → 250,000 enrolled → founded Howard University (1867), one of first HBCUs.
p2: Distributed 21 million rations of food to freedmen → provided basic housing, medical care and legal support.
p3: Closure 1872 → gains immediately reversed → educational and social progress lost without federal infrastructure to sustain it.

front: What was the impact of KKK terror during and after Reconstruction?
p1: KKK founded Tennessee 1865 → used violence to intimidate African Americans from voting, education, asserting rights.
p2: Colfax Massacre (1873) → c.100 African Americans killed in Louisiana following contested elections → federal government failed to help. New Orleans Massacre (1866): 40–200 killed.
p3: Enforcement Acts (1870–71) → Grant suppressed 1st KKK → over 600 prosecuted. But after 1877 troop withdrawal → KKK resurgent + unpunished.

front: What was the impact of lynching on African American social rights?
p1: Lynching epidemic → 100+ per year in early 1890s → used as tool of racial terror to enforce social hierarchy and deter political participation.
p2: Ida B. Wells → 'Southern Horrors' (1892) → documented frequency + disproved myth it was response to violent crime → national + international campaign.
p3: Southern Democratic politicians repeatedly defeated anti-lynching bills in Congress. In 1900, Governor Tillman of South Carolina openly defended lynching.

front: What was the impact of convict leasing on African Americans?
p1: Exploited 13th Amendment loophole → 'except as punishment for crime' → Southern states arrested African Americans on trivial charges → leased to private companies as unpaid labour.
p2: Grew across the South in the 1880s → effectively recreated slavery → dangerous conditions, no pay, no rights.
p3: System designed to control Black population + provide cheap labour to Southern economies → continued into early 20th century.

front: What was the role of anti-civil rights groups in hindering African American rights?
p1: KKK → violence at poll booths, lynching, destruction of Black organisations → Colfax Massacre (1873): 100+ killed to prevent voting.
p2: White Citizens Councils (1955) → 'respectable' opposition to integration → pressured employers, banks and landlords to discriminate → counterpart to KKK in the 1950s–60s.
p3: United Daughters of the Confederacy → 'Lost Cause' myth → romanticised slavery + Confederacy → justified Jim Crow → shaped Southern white opinion for generations.

front: What ideas and attitudes were used to justify Jim Crow?
p1: Lost Cause myth: United Daughters of the Confederacy romanticised slavery as noble — framed Civil War as states' rights struggle, not slavery. Justified Jim Crow as preserving natural social order. Confederate monuments, school textbooks and Birth of a Nation (1915) spread the mythology nationally.
p2: Social Darwinism: pseudoscientific extension of Darwin's theories — framed African Americans as 'backward', on inferior rung of civilisation. Eugenic theories seen as modern science. Justified racial separation as natural progress. Provided intellectual respectability for white supremacy.
p3: Religious justification: many white Southern Christians believed racial hierarchy divinely ordained — Richmond Times editor: 'God almighty drew the color line.' Churches supported segregation. Lost Cause gave historical justification → Social Darwinism gave scientific justification → religion gave divine justification.
hints: God almighty drew the color line

front: What was the significance of Birth of a Nation (1915) and the rise of the second KKK?
p1: Birth of a Nation (1915): D.W. Griffith film — glorified first KKK, depicted Black men as violent sexual predators. Screened at White House by Wilson who praised it. Led directly to KKK revival.
p2: Second KKK: membership reached 5 million by 1920s — 15% of population. Unlike first KKK, national not just Southern — included politicians, police chiefs, judges across North and West. Targeted Catholics, Jews and immigrants as well as African Americans.
p3: Impact: 1925 — Klan burned crosses outside NAACP offices. KKK members in public office undermined law enforcement against racial violence. Showed white supremacy was national not uniquely Southern — critical challenge to Great Migration narrative.

front: What was the impact of WWI on African Americans?
p1: 380,000 African Americans served in segregated units → Harlem Hellfighters → stationed in Britain, experienced less segregated society → raised expectations. Wartime demand for labour → Great Migration accelerated → 500,000 moved North 1916–19.
p2: NAACP membership grew as African Americans demanded rights in exchange for war service → Double V Campaign foundations laid. Economic wages in Northern factories far above sharecropping — temporary but transformative shift.
p3: Red Summer (1919) → return of white soldiers + industrial retraction → race riots in 25+ cities. Elaine Massacre (1919): 200+ Black sharecroppers killed for organising for better wages. Gains were short-lived — showed wartime opportunity did not translate to lasting rights.

front: What was the significance of the Harlem Renaissance?
p1: 1920s cultural explosion → Langston Hughes, Louis Armstrong, Zora Neale Hurston → Black artistic achievement gained national recognition.
p2: Harlem population grew 50,000 → 200,000 (1910–1930) → Du Bois used The Crisis to promote Black intellectualism → 100,000 circulation.
p3: Cultural flourishing did not translate into political or economic gains → KKK at 5 million same decade → Tulsa massacre (1921) destroyed 'Black Wall Street'.

front: What was the impact of the Tulsa Race Massacre (1921)?
p1: White mob destroyed Greenwood District ('Black Wall Street') → 600+ Black-owned businesses destroyed → 35 blocks burned.
p2: Up to 300 African Americans killed → 10,000 left homeless → one of worst incidents of racial violence in US history.
p3: Showed that Black economic success provoked violent white backlash → prosperity offered no protection without political and legal rights.

front: What was the impact of the Great Depression on African Americans?
p1: Black unemployment 50% vs 25% national average → 75% of Southern African Americans still sharecroppers → urban Black unemployment reached 20% in Chicago vs 12% white — before Depression.
p2: AFL had no affiliated Black unions → African Americans restricted to unprotected jobs → no Social Security for agricultural/domestic workers. NOI founded (1930) → offered alternative social and economic vision of Black self-reliance.
p3: 50+ African Americans lynched annually in late 1920s → KKK 5 million members → social conditions deteriorated. BUT Great Depression shifted African Americans into Democratic coalition → produced New Deal federal pressure.

front: What was the significance of the Double V Campaign and WWII service?
p1: NAACP launched Double V → victory against fascism abroad AND racism at home → exposed contradiction of fighting for democracy while denying it domestically.
p2: NAACP membership grew 50,000 → 500,000 during WWII → Cold War context made federal government increasingly conscious of international optics.
p3: Soviet propaganda publicised racial violence like Birmingham Campaign → Kennedy: 'We preach freedom around the world… but are we to say the land of the free — except for the negroes?'

front: What was the impact of the Emmett Till case (1955)?
p1: 14-year-old boy from Chicago murdered in Mississippi → body mutilated → murderers acquitted by all-white jury.
p2: Mother insisted on open-casket funeral → allowed media to share images of Emmett's body → spread outrage nationally and internationally.
p3: Galvanised civil rights movement → demonstrated that racial terror was ongoing + systemic → key catalyst for Montgomery Bus Boycott.

front: What was the role of Cold War context in advancing African American civil rights?
p1: Soviet propaganda publicised US racial violence to discredit America internationally → Birmingham Campaign broadcast globally.
p2: Federal Government increasingly conscious of Cold War optics → Kennedy: 'land of the free — except for the negroes?' after Birmingham.
p3: Decolonisation movements in 1950s–60s inspired African Americans → Gandhi + Kwame Nkrumah's actions influenced non-violent strategy.

front: What was the role of the media in advancing the Civil Rights Movement?
p1: Televised images of Bloody Sunday (1965) + Birmingham Campaign (1963) shocked international audiences → generated massive support for movement.
p2: King adept at exploiting television cameras → chose Birmingham deliberately because Bull Connor guaranteed visible brutality → forced federal response.
p3: Emmett Till's open casket (1955) → media images of body spread outrage. Contrast with 19th century press → had perpetuated stereotypes + justified lynching.

front: What was the impact of Vietnam War on the Civil Rights Movement?
p1: African Americans disproportionately drafted → returned radicalised + disillusioned → fed Black Power ethos of militancy.
p2: King's 'Beyond Vietnam' speech (1967) → severed relationship with LBJ → ended federal momentum on civil rights reforms.
p3: Media attention shifted from civil rights marches to anti-war protests → movement lost national spotlight → Black Power filled the vacuum.

front: What was the impact of the Black Panther Party's community programmes?
p1: Free breakfast programmes → fed 20,000 children per day → 'survival programmes' addressed poverty the civil rights legislation had not solved.
p2: 13 health clinics established → screened thousands for sickle cell anaemia → People's Free Medical Centres in 13 deprived areas. 60+ community schools.
p3: BPP's 10-Point Programme demanded reparations, land, full employment, decent housing → shifted civil rights agenda from legal equality to economic justice.

front: What were the Long Hot Summers (1967) and what caused them?
p1: 150 race riots in 1967 → largest in Detroit and Newark → response to poverty, police brutality and de facto segregation in Northern cities.
p2: Watts (1965) $40m property damage → exposed failure of non-violence + civil rights legislation to address systemic Northern inequality.
p3: Showed CRM had not resolved economic grievances → MLK's assassination (1968) triggered new wave of riots → Nixon won on 'Law and Order' ticket.

front: What was the impact of COINTELPRO on Black Power organisations?
p1: FBI infiltrated Black Power groups → planted informants → manufactured evidence → created internal suspicion + divisions.
p2: Arrests + assassinations: Fred Hampton (Black Panther leader) killed in FBI-orchestrated raid 1969 → Panthers collapsed by 1982.
p3: Panthers never exceeded 5,000 members → COINTELPRO accelerated collapse → demonstrated state willingness to use illegal tactics against civil rights organisations.

front: What was the significance of the Los Angeles Riots (1992)?
p1: Erupted after acquittal of LAPD officers for beating Rodney King by all-white jury → $1 billion of damage → 63 killed.
p2: Demonstrated that police brutality + racial injustice remained systemic → civil rights legislation had not changed ground realities for urban Black communities.
p3: Positive strides by 1992 → Oprah, Michael Jordan, Spike Lee as icons of Black success → but persistent stereotypes + poverty for majority remained.

front: Why did sharecropping trap African Americans in poverty?
p1: No land redistribution → '40 acres and a mule' never realised → freedpeople forced to farm same land, same landowner as during slavery.
p2: Crop-lien system → sharecroppers paid rent in crops → always in debt to landowner → could not leave without repaying debt → effective debt bondage.
p3: By 1900 only 25% of African Americans owned land → economic freedom impossible without land ownership → Southern economic system rebuilt on near-slavery.

front: What evidence is there of Black economic success during the Gilded Age?
p1: Parallel businesses emerged in the de jure segregated South — 50,000+ Black-owned businesses by 1890s including grocery stores, laundrettes, barbershops and 40 Black-owned banks. 'Black towns' like Mound Bayou, Mississippi had 150+ Black businesses. Booker T. Washington's Negro Business League (1900) had 600 chapters.
p2: By 1900, c.50,000 African American professionals including doctors, lawyers and teachers (out of a population of 8 million). Literacy rate rose from 10% (1865) to 50% (1900). African American landownership reached 15 million acres by early 20th century — up from almost nothing in 1865.
p3: Limitations: 90% of African Americans still lived in the South as agricultural labourers by 1900. Sharecropping and the crop-lien system kept most in poverty — by 1900 only 25% owned land. Economic success was fragile and vulnerable to white backlash — Tulsa (1921) showed Black Wall Street could be destroyed overnight.

front: What was the significance of the Great Migration?
p1: 1916–1970 → over 6 million African Americans moved from rural South to Northern + Western cities → escaping Jim Crow + seeking economic opportunity.
p2: Created influential Black urban communities → Harlem + South Side Chicago → fostered cultural and political movements → WWI phase: 500,000 moved 1916–19.
p3: Opened skilled industrial jobs in North → 40% of Black men in North held skilled jobs by 1920 vs 15% in South → but de facto segregation + racial hostility persisted.

front: How did the First New Deal affect African Americans economically?
p1: FERA → direct relief → 20–30% of recipients were African American. CCC → employed c.200,000 African Americans (10% of enrolment). PWA → 65,000+ in infrastructure jobs by 1940.
p2: Some Black sharecroppers became independent farmers through federal assistance → Black Cabinet influenced programme delivery.
p3: AAA (1933) inadvertently displaced 200,000 Black sharecroppers → NRA codes manipulated by employers → gains were partial and unevenly distributed.

front: How did the Second New Deal affect African Americans?
p1: WPA → infrastructure jobs → 15% of workers were African American. Social Security Act → pensions + unemployment insurance for the first time.
p2: Wagner Act (1935) → recognised BSCP → first Black union to win AFL recognition → but inadvertently created 'closed shops' → white-only unions could dominate.
p3: Bethune's role in NYA → funded training + jobs for 600,000 Black youths during Depression → most direct targeted benefit for African Americans.

front: What were the economic limitations of the New Deal for African Americans?
p1: Social Security excluded agricultural + domestic workers → 65% of Black workers → most significant exclusion from New Deal economic protection.
p2: Aid administered by Southern states → whites controlled distribution → African Americans discriminated against in application of relief policies.
p3: Anti-Communist Red Scare → organisations advocating for Black economic rights suspected of communism → CIO lost funding → unions weakened.

front: What was the impact of Executive Order 8802 (1941)?
p1: Randolph's March on Washington Movement threatened 100,000-strong march → pressured FDR → EO 8802 banned racial discrimination in defence industries.
p2: By end of WWII → 2 million+ African Americans employed in defence industries → significant wartime economic opportunity.
p3: First time a mass non-violent movement forced a major federal economic concession → model for later civil rights pressure tactics.

front: What were the post-war economic challenges facing African Americans?
p1: GI Bill (1944): provided education, housing loans and job training to veterans — but administered locally in the South → African American veterans denied benefits. Restrictive covenants barred Black veterans from suburban housing (e.g. Levittown). White veterans built wealth through homeownership; Black veterans locked out.
p2: Automation: post-WWII manufacturing shift disproportionately hit African Americans concentrated in low-skill manual jobs. Black unemployment double white unemployment. Manufacturing jobs eliminated were precisely those gained during Great Migration and wartime production.
p3: Continued violence: NAACP recorded 56 Black veterans attacked, some in uniform, in 1919. Pattern repeated post-WWII — returning veterans who asserted rights targeted. Economic exclusion compounded by residential segregation in the North and West.

front: What was the impact of the Great Society programmes on African American economic rights?
p1: Medicare + Medicaid (1965) → Black Americans with health insurance: 25% → 75% by 1970. Food Stamp Act (1964) → 33% of recipients were African American despite being 12% of population.
p2: Civil Rights Act (1964) → prohibited employment discrimination → EEOC enforcement → African Americans in white-collar jobs: 5% (1960) → 15% (mid-1970s).
p3: Despite legislation → by 1970 Black families earned average 58% of white families → CRM failed to make economic gains in Northern cities.

front: What was the impact of affirmative action on African American economic rights?
p1: First introduced Philadelphia 1969 → spread nationally → African Americans in white-collar jobs: 5% (1960) → 15% (mid-1970s) → growing Black middle class.
p2: Regents of University of California v Bakke (1978) → racial quotas unconstitutional → weakened programme. Reagan/Bush labelled it 'reverse discrimination' → federal enforcement reduced.
p3: By 1980s → 40% of African Americans middle class → but gains uneven → 'bifurcation' → persistent ghetto poverty alongside professional success.

front: What was the economic position of African Americans by 1992?
p1: African Americans earned 60% of average white income → Black unemployment 14.2% vs 7.2% white → overrepresented in low-wage sectors.
p2: Homeownership 43% vs 70% white → redlining + discriminatory lending had lasting effects → urban renewal projects displaced many Black communities.
p3: 500,000+ Black-owned businesses → $10 billion gross revenue → 40% middle class → but 33% below poverty line → 'bifurcation' defined economic reality by 1992.

front: How different were experiences of African Americans outside of the South during the Gilded Age?
p1: North → better industrial jobs + education → growing Black middle class → BUT de facto segregation — Chicago 5,000 confined to one area; NY Harlem separate district for 23,000 → white unions hostile → most in menial jobs
p2: West → relative racial indifference → cowboys, trappers, miners, shopkeepers → Bass Reeves: Deputy US Marshal, arrested thousands → Mary Fields: famous stagecoach driver → all-Black towns: Allensworth CA, Dearfield CO
p3: Limits → Exoduster movement (1879): 40,000 fled South to Kansas → faced hostility + hardship → racial violence still present → by 1900, 90% of African Americans still in the South — North/West were exceptions

front: What was the significance of key Supreme Court cases during the Gilded Age?
p1: States' Rights doctrine → Supreme Court ruled 14th Amendment only protected national citizenship → states free to discriminate → gave constitutional backing to white supremacy throughout the Gilded Age
p2: Plessy v Ferguson (1896) → 'separate but equal' constitutional → Jim Crow legal cover for 58 years → Cumming v Richmond (1899): upheld unequal schools — Black high school closed, white remained open
p3: Mississippi v Williams (1898) → upheld literacy tests + poll taxes → by 1900, 90% of Southern African Americans disenfranchised → Supreme Court = instrument of oppression, not protection

front: What was the significance of W.E.B. Du Bois?
p1: First Black Harvard PhD (1895) → Niagara Movement (1905): demanded full civil + political rights, directly opposed Washington → co-founded NAACP (1909) → The Crisis: 100,000 subscribers by 1920
p2: 'Talented tenth' → educated Black professional class to lead liberation through intellect + political agitation → Pan-Africanism: organised Pan-African Congresses 1919, 1921, 1923 → linked AA struggle to global anti-colonialism
p3: Limits → middle-class focus → struggled to connect with poorest African Americans → socialist leanings → FBI surveillance during Red Scare → emigrated to Ghana 1961, disillusioned with American racism

front: How strong was the position of African Americans by 1932?
p1: Progress: literacy 10% (1865) → 85% (1930) → 300,000 in Northern schools → NAACP won US v Guinn (1915) removing grandfather clauses → Great Migration created Harlem Renaissance → some Black political representation in North
p2: Weakness: only 2% registered to vote in South → 75% still sharecroppers → Black unemployment 50% vs 25% national (Depression) → KKK 15% of eligible population → 50+ lynchings/year in 1920s
p3: Structural limits: anti-lynching bills repeatedly blocked → Reconstruction gains fully reversed in South → NAACP legal successes but no political power → 90% still in South with no vote, land or security

front: Was Roosevelt's administration an effective supporter of African American rights?
p1: Effective: appointed more Black Americans to gov than any predecessor → Black Cabinet led by Bethune → Eleanor Roosevelt resigned DAR to support Marian Anderson (1939) → Hastie: first Black federal judge 1937 → NYA trained 600,000 Black youths
p2: Political shift: ¾ AA voted Republican 1932 → ¾ voted Democrat 1936 → fundamental realignment → WPA employed 1 million+ AA by 1939 → Harold Ickes pushed anti-segregation policies
p3: Ineffective: refused anti-lynching bill — feared losing Southern Democrats → AAA displaced 200,000 Black sharecroppers → Social Security excluded 65% of Black workers → CCC segregated → civil rights consistently side-lined

front: What was the cultural impact of Black Power?
p1: Black Arts Movement (1965–75): Amiri Baraka founded Black Arts Repertory Theatre 1965 — 'cultural wing of Black Power' → 500+ Black arts organisations → James Brown 'Say It Loud — I'm Black and I'm Proud' (1968)
p2: 500+ Black Studies programmes in US universities by 1971 → demanded by student activists → Afro hairstyle, dashikis = acts of political assertion → 'Black is Beautiful' challenged white beauty standards
p3: Limits → cultural gains did not translate to economic/political progress → mainly felt by middle-class + educated → those in ghettos saw little change → COINTELPRO destroyed key cultural organisations alongside political ones

front: What was the role of State Governments in hindering African Americans during the Gilded Age?
p1: Black Codes (1865–6) → restricted movement, labour and assembly of freedmen → de facto re-enslavement before federal repeal → after Compromise of 1877: Jim Crow laws spread across South from 1877 → segregated every area of public life
p2: Voter suppression: Mississippi (1890) → literacy tests, poll taxes, grandfather clauses → Black voter registration: 90% (1867) → 6% (1892) → spread across South → Mississippi v Williams (1898) upheld these methods
p3: State govts took no action on racial violence → Governor Tillman SC openly defended lynching (1900) → 1,875 lynchings in 1890s alone → Wilmington Coup (1898): white supremacists overthrew biracial elected government → state actors = perpetrators not protectors

front: What was the position of labour and union rights in 1865?
p1: No legal protections for unions — courts upheld employers' right to suppress organising. 20 state governments had laws allowing militias to intervene in labour disputes. No obligation for employers to recognise unions.
p2: NLU (1866): 300,000 members at peak — but collapsed after Sylvis's death (1869). Craft unions like Cigar Makers represented less than 10% of workers in any industry. Fewer than 5% of strikes led to concessions 1865–75.
p3: Working conditions dire: 3,000 railroad workers killed and 20,000 injured annually in early 1870s. 750,000 children under 15 in industrial labour. Immigrants worked 60–70 hours/week for as little as $1/day. No injury compensation.

front: What was the significance of the Great Railroad Strike (1877)?
p1: Spontaneous nationwide strike following wage cuts during economic depression — spread from West Virginia across the country. Workers from different railroads shut down rail traffic.
p2: Federal troops called in — killed over 100 workers. Government's focus on maintaining order rather than addressing workers' grievances.
p3: First nationwide labour dispute → exposed need for stronger organised unions → showed federal violent resistance was the government's default response to strikes.

front: What was the significance of the NLU, CNLU and KOL in early industrialisation?
p1: NLU (1866): first national labour organisation — Sylvis pushed for 8-hour workday and legislative reforms. Undermined by economic depression of early 1870s and internal divisions — over-reliant on Sylvis, collapsed 1869.
p2: CNLU (1869): formed by African American workers excluded from NLU — showed racial divisions embedded from the start. KOL (1869): most inclusive early union — welcomed skilled and unskilled, women, African Americans and immigrants.
p3: Molly Maguires (1873): violent conflicts in Pennsylvania coalfields — Pinkerton agents infiltrated, 10 leaders executed 1876. Associated unions with violence — damaged public support.

front: What was the significance of the Haymarket Affair (1886) and the collapse of the KOL?
p1: KOL grew from 20,000 (1881) to 700,000 (1886) — most inclusive labour organisation, welcomed women, African Americans and immigrants. Rally in Chicago demanding 8-hour workday turned violent — bomb killed 7 police officers.
p2: KOL collapsed — associated with radicalism and anarchism. AFL (1886) established as safer alternative under Gompers — focused on skilled workers only, excluded unskilled, women and most African Americans.
p3: Haymarket associated industrial unionism with anarchism in public mind — damaged union movement for decades. Showed employer and government hostility could destroy even a 700,000-strong organisation.

front: What was the significance of the Homestead Strike (1892)?
p1: Carnegie Steel locked out Amalgamated Association workers — wage cuts + anti-union. 300 Pinkerton agents arrived by barge, 12 dead in violent clash. 8,000 state militia deployed — workers defeated.
p2: AFL refused to support — exposed skilled/unskilled division. Steel industry union-free until 1930s. Homestead virtually bankrupted the union. Carnegie's absence in Scotland damaged his 'workers' friend' reputation.
p3: Showed corporations would use private armies and state force against workers. Highlighted Gilded Age employer power. Contrast: Flint sit-down (1936–37) finally won UAW recognition — over 40 years later.

front: What was the role of the AFL during the Gilded Age?
p1: Founded 1886 by Samuel Gompers — focused on skilled workers, pushed for higher wages, shorter workdays and better conditions through collective bargaining rather than confrontation. Made some gains negotiating with Hanna and JP Morgan.
p2: Exclusionary by design — neglected unskilled labourers, women and most African Americans. AFL included 60,000 Black workers by late 19th century but no Black union won a charter until BSCP in 1930s.
p3: Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) routinely used against unions as illegal restraints of trade. By end of century trade union membership reached 500,000 — but only 500,000 of a workforce of millions, mostly in skilled trades.

front: What was the significance of the Great Coal Strike (1902)?
p1: 140,000 miners — demanded higher wages, shorter hours and union recognition. President Roosevelt intervened to arbitrate rather than send troops — first time federal government acted as mediator not suppressor.
p2: Mitchell's moderate UMWA leadership secured presidential support — Roosevelt more sympathetic to Mitchell than the abrasive company owners. Owners agreed to wage increase and improved conditions.
p3: Partial success — marked shift in Progressive Era attitude. BUT no formal union recognition. Showed moderate leadership could achieve more than confrontation. First positive federal intervention in a labour dispute.

front: What was the significance of the IWW and the Lawrence Textile Strike (1912)?
p1: IWW ('Wobblies') founded 1905 — sought to unite all workers regardless of skill, including immigrants and minorities. Open to groups excluded by AFL. Association with socialism and anarchism led to government suppression.
p2: Lawrence Textile 'Bread and Roses' Strike (1912): immigrant women from multiple ethnic groups — IWW-led. Women received 15% pay rise and overtime pay. No reprisal agreement against strikers — step forward for right to strike.
p3: Showed power of solidarity across ethnic lines. BUT IWW's radical tactics ultimately led to its suppression — radical methods alienated moderates. Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911): 146 garment workers killed — galvanised demand for safety laws.

front: What was the impact of WWI and the Red Scare on labour rights?
p1: NWLB (1918): agreement between employers and AFL to maintain production — temporarily legitimised unions and facilitated collective bargaining. BUT policies only benefited AFL — excluded unskilled and unaffiliated workers.
p2: AFL agreed no-strike pledges during WWI — prioritised national unity. Seattle General Strike (1919): 65,000 workers — suppressed by Mayor Hanson, demonised by media as Bolshevist. Red Scare: union activity viewed as communist threat.
p3: Red Summer (1919): race riots across major US cities — economic tensions between Black and white workers competing for jobs. Post-war reversal — all wartime gains quickly rolled back. Workers' sacrifices during war brought no lasting rights.

front: What was the impact of welfare capitalism on labour rights in the 1920s?
p1: Employers introduced pensions, healthcare and benefits — reduced perceived need for unions. Yellow-dog contracts widespread — workers signed away right to join unions as condition of employment. Company unions replaced independent ones.
p2: Union membership declined from peak of 5 million (1920). Deering v Duplex (1921): restricted secondary boycotts. Adkins v Children's Hospital (1923): struck down minimum wage for women — 'freedom of contract' doctrine.
p3: BSCP founded 1925 by Philip Randolph — first successful Black union, sought recognition from Pullman Company and AFL. Would not achieve it until 1937. Wall St Crash (1929): unemployment 25% — ended welfare capitalism era abruptly.

front: What was the significance of the Wagner Act (1935)?
p1: Guaranteed right to unionise and collectively bargain — established NLRB to enforce. Banned company spies, company unions, blacklisting and dismissal of union organisers. Union membership: 3 million (1933) → 8 million (1940).
p2: Wagner Act promoted closed shops — but this inadvertently excluded Black workers from AFL unions. Social Security (1935) excluded farm and domestic workers — 65% of Black workers. Henry Ford resisted UAW recognition until 1941.
p3: Milestone in labour rights — first time federal government legally recognised workers' right to organise. BUT relied on Southern Democrats who used local administration to undermine it. Employer resistance continued through spy networks and blacklisting.

front: What was the significance of the CIO and the Flint Sit-Down Strike (1936–37)?
p1: John Lewis formed CIO (1935) as part of AFL — focused on industrial workers regardless of skill, including women and African Americans. AFL expelled CIO in 1938 — exposed fractures in movement.
p2: Flint Sit-Down Strike (1936–37): 40,000 workers at General Motors — CIO-led. Workers occupied the factory rather than picketing outside — harder to replace. Forced recognition of UAW. Inspired 200 more sit-down strikes in 1937.
p3: US Steel unionised 1937 without a strike — over 40 years after Homestead failure. NLRB v Fansteel (1939): sit-down strikes ruled illegal. Memorial Day Massacre (1937): Chicago police killed 10 striking steelworkers — public outrage strengthened solidarity.

front: What was the significance of Philip Randolph and the BSCP?
p1: BSCP founded 1925 — first successful Black union. Randolph became first African American to lead a national union that won a collective bargaining agreement. AFL recognition achieved 1935, Pullman Company recognition 1937.
p2: March on Washington Movement (1941): threatened 100,000-strong march on Washington — pressured Roosevelt to issue EO 8802, prohibiting racial discrimination in defence industries. First time a mass non-violent movement forced a major federal concession.
p3: Significance beyond labour: demonstrated power of non-violent mass pressure — model later used by civil rights movement. BSCP's success relied on shift in federal attitudes with New Deal. Showed Black workers could win through organisation rather than confrontation.

front: What was the impact of the Taft-Hartley Act (1947)?
p1: Passed over Truman's veto — amended Wagner Act. Banned secondary strikes and closed shops. Allowed states to pass right-to-work laws prohibiting mandatory union membership — 21 states enacted them, primarily in South and West.
p2: Required union leaders to sign anti-communist oaths — fostered division within movement, weakened CIO whose leaders included communists. McCarthyism (Red Scare 1946–50s): union activism linked to communism — further undermined left-leaning unions.
p3: Post-WWII strike wave (1946): 5,000 strikes involving 4.6 million workers — showed pent-up pressure. Taft-Hartley imposed 60-day cooling-off period for strikes threatening national security. Marked beginning of rollback from WWII peak of 35% union membership.

front: What was the significance of the AFL-CIO merger (1955)?
p1: AFL and CIO merged — 16 million members, representing 85% of unionised workforce. Combined both craft and industrial unions into one huge negotiating bloc. AFL-CIO members earned 20% more than non-unionised workers by 1960s.
p2: Automation 1950s–60s: manufacturing job losses — blue-collar unions weakened. New white-collar workers uninterested in labour struggle. New electronics and service sectors relocated to avoid unions. Manufacturing declined 40% from 1970 peak by 1979.
p3: OSHA (1970): established workplace safety standards — significantly reduced workplace injuries and deaths. Civil Rights Act (1964): prohibited employment discrimination by race, sex or national origin. Kennedy EO 10988 (1962): federal employees right to unionise.

front: What was the significance of Cesar Chavez and the UFW?
p1: UFW (1966): Chavez organised Filipino and Mexican American farm workers — historically without union representation, excluded from most labour legislation. Delano Grape Strike (1965–70): nationwide grape boycott forced collective bargaining agreement.
p2: Salad Bowl Strike (1970): led by Filipino workers, supported by Mexican and other ethnic groups. Success — strengthened UFW's position, led to better wages and union recognition for farm workers. California Agricultural Relations Board (1975): UFW victory.
p3: Showed power of nonviolent strikes and consumer boycotts beyond the workplace. Expanded labour movement beyond its traditional white male industrial base — major increase in Hispanic union membership. UFW model influenced subsequent immigrant labour organising.

front: What was the significance of DRUM and the LRBW?
p1: DRUM (1968): established in Detroit to push for racial equality for Black workers in auto industry — organised wildcat strikes at Chrysler's Dodge Main plant. 500+ members by 1969. Inspired FRUM, CADRUM and GRUM across Detroit industries.
p2: LRBW pushed for Black leadership in UAW — Black workers made up 30% of UAW membership by early 1970s but leadership representation still limited. Black workers earned $2,000 less per year than white counterparts in late 1960s.
p3: Limits: UAW leadership resistant to wildcat tactics despite similar methods having founded CIO in 1930s. LRBW collapsed from internal divisions — unable to resolve racial vs class basis of struggle. Showed limits of Black Power's intersection with organised labour.

front: What was the impact of the PATCO Strike (1981)?
p1: Air traffic controllers struck for $10,000 pay rise, improved conditions and reduced hours. Reagan declared strike illegal — fired 11,000 workers and banned them from federal employment. Effectively decertified the union.
p2: Marked decisive shift in balance of power between government and unions — emboldened employers across all industries to adopt anti-union stances. Union-busting became standard practice. Outsourcing and non-unionised temporary workers normalised.
p3: PATCO alienated public — seen as demanding excessive pay rise during summer holidays, making Reagan's response politically easy. Union membership: 24% (1979) → 16% (1990). Most damaging single act of government hostility to unions since Pullman (1894).

front: What was the position of labour and union rights by 1992?
p1: Union membership 16% of workforce — down from 35% (1945) and 24% (1979). Deindustrialisation, automation and globalisation eroded traditional union base. Manufacturing jobs declined 40% from 1970 peak.
p2: Legal framework survived: Wagner Act, NLRB, OSHA, Civil Rights Act (1964), Equal Pay Act (1963) all in force. But employers routinely used union-busting consultants and relocated to right-to-work states. Strike activity fell dramatically from 1981.
p3: AFL-CIO members still earned more than non-unionised workers but gap narrowing. Women and minority workers still disproportionately in non-unionised, lower-paid roles. Racial disparities in wages and union leadership persisted into 1980s.

front: What were working conditions like during the Gilded Age?
p1: 2,000 rail workers killed in accidents in 1889 alone → by 1900, 35,000 workplace deaths annually → no federal safety legislation. Panic of 1873: long depression — wages dropped by nearly half. In 1892 alone the National Guard used 23 times to break strikes.
p2: Women 15% of industrial workforce — earned $3–6/week vs $7–10 for men. Immigrants 15–20% of urban industrial workforce — worked 60–70 hours/week for as little as $1/day. In cotton mills, children as young as 8 worked 12-hour shifts for $1/week. 750,000 children under 15 in industrial labour.
p3: Unskilled workers earned only 30% of skilled workers' wages. 2% of population owned 30% of wealth. No legal framework for employer-provided benefits — injured workers left destitute. Blacklisting shared among 50 mine operators in Pennsylvania.

front: What was the significance of Eugene Debs and the ARU?
p1: ARU (1894): first successful industrial union — mobilised railroad workers across industries regardless of skill. Debs led Pullman Strike (1894) — although defeated, brought national attention to plight of workers.
p2: Debs' advocacy for socialism led him to run for president multiple times as Socialist Party candidate — won 6% of vote in 1912. Imprisoned for Pullman strike role — became symbol of labour martyrdom.
p3: ARU showed potential of industrial unionism — organising workers across all industries within a sector. BUT AFL refused to support ARU during Pullman strike — skilled/unskilled division fatally weakened it. Court injunction set precedent used to break future strikes.

front: What was the role of divisions within the Gilded Age labour movement?
p1: Skilled vs unskilled: AFL excluded unskilled workers — Pullman Strike (1894) failed partly because AFL refused to support ARU. KOL collapsed not just from Haymarket but from poor organisation and internal conflicts.
p2: Racial division: NLU excluded Black workers → CNLU formed separately (1869). African Americans used as strike-breakers — exacerbated mistrust. Chinese Exclusion Act (1882) — passed with KOL support — marginalised Chinese workers.
p3: 11 million new immigrants from southern and eastern Europe → race to the bottom on wages → nativist hostility within unions. Immigrant willingness to accept low wages angered native-born workers. Fewer than 5% of strikes led to concessions 1865–75 — lack of solidarity a root cause.

front: What was the role of the courts and legislation in shaping labour rights in the Progressive Era?
p1: Lochner v New York (1905): Supreme Court struck down law limiting bakers' working hours — 'freedom of contract' doctrine used to block protective legislation. Coppage v Kansas (1915): upheld yellow-dog contracts — workers could be forced to agree not to join unions.
p2: Clayton Antitrust Act (1914): attempted to exempt unions from antitrust laws, preventing courts using injunctions against strikes. BUT Duplex Printing Press v Deering (1921) later limited its impact — injunctions against unions continued.
p3: Keating-Owen Child Labour Act (1916): prohibited child labour in interstate commerce — struck down by Supreme Court 1918. Wilson established Department of Labor (1913) — Cabinet-level position for first time. Courts remained hostile tool of employers throughout Progressive Era.

front: What was the significance of the Seattle General Strike (1919)?
p1: 65,000 workers across various industries struck in solidarity — largest general strike in US history to that point. Aimed to show power of cross-industry solidarity beyond a single workplace dispute.
p2: Suppressed by Mayor Ole Hanson — described as a Bolshevist revolution. Media demonised strikers as anarchists and communists. Failed to achieve aims — exposed limits of general strike as tactic in hostile political climate.
p3: Red Scare (1919): Bolshevik Revolution in Russia sparked fears of global communist revolution — union activity viewed with deep suspicion. All post-WWI labour gains rapidly reversed. Showed that wartime solidarity had not translated into political power for unions.

front: What was the impact of the Great Depression on labour rights?
p1: Wall St Crash (1929) → unemployment rose to 25% nationally — 50% for African Americans. Bargaining power of workers collapsed. Demand for federal reform grew — existing union structure could not respond.
p2: Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932): prohibited federal courts from using injunctions against peaceful strikes and banned yellow-dog contracts — first significant legislative gain in decades. Unions had only 3 million members by 1932 — a fraction of the workforce.
p3: Great Depression created conditions for New Deal — showed welfare capitalism had failed. Workers' desperation drove Flint sit-down strikes and pressure for Wagner Act. In 1932, ¾ of African Americans still voted Republican — political realignment not yet complete.

front: What was the significance of the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938)?
p1: $25 weekly minimum wage established — first federal minimum wage. Maximum working hours legislated. Child labour under 16 banned in industries engaged in interstate commerce.
p2: Passed despite opposition from business groups — showed New Deal coalition could overcome employer resistance. PWA, CCC and WPA had already created millions of jobs — FLSA entrenched gains in law.
p3: Limits: did not address gender pay gap — women still earned significantly less than men. Excluded farm and domestic workers — sectors with large proportion of Black and immigrant workers. Employers exploited loopholes to avoid compliance.

front: What was the impact of McCarthyism on the labour movement?
p1: Second Red Scare (1946–50s): union activism linked to communism — crackdown on perceived communist influence. Taft-Hartley Act (1947) required union leaders to sign anti-communist oaths — those who refused could not use NLRB.
p2: CIO weakened — many left-wing unions expelled or forced to purge communist members. Divisions between anti-communist and left-wing unions undermined movement solidarity. Landrum-Griffin Act (1959) further curtailed unions' political activities.
p3: Long-term damage: labour movement's political influence narrowed — no longer able to advocate for broader social change without being labelled communist. Chilled union organising in public sector and new industries. AFL-CIO merger (1955) partly a response — combined strength to resist Red Scare pressure.

front: What was the impact of automation and deindustrialisation on labour rights?
p1: Automation 1950s–60s: eliminated many manual jobs — blue-collar unions weakened as manufacturing workforce shrank. Rise of white-collar workers who were uninterested in the labour struggle and difficult to organise.
p2: By 1979, manufacturing jobs had declined 40% from 1970 peak. New electronics and service sectors relocated to avoid unions — moved to Southwest US with weak union presence. Globalisation: outsourcing to countries with cheaper labour eroded union power in traditional industries.
p3: Unions struggled to adapt — collective bargaining built around manufacturing not applicable to service industries. Union membership began long decline from peak of 35% (1945). Contrast with 1960s when AFL-CIO members earned 20% more than non-unionised workers — gap narrowed by 1980s.

front: What was the impact of the gender and racial divisions in the post-war labour movement?
p1: Women excluded from many unions for much of the 19th and early 20th centuries — expected to form separate, less influential organisations. After WWII, unions reluctant to accept women as full members. Women in lower-paying, non-unionised roles disproportionately.
p2: Racial divisions persisted: no Black union won an AFL charter until BSCP in 1930s. UAW leadership resistant to DRUM's wildcat tactics (1968) despite similar methods having founded the CIO. Black workers still earned $2,000 less per year than white counterparts in late 1960s.
p3: Coalition of Labor Union Women (1974): national organisation advocating for working women. Civil Rights Act (1964): prohibited employment discrimination by race, sex or national origin — significant for both women and Black workers. Equal Pay Act (1963): mandated equal pay. Progress slow — disparities in wages, jobs and union leadership persisted into 1980s.

front: What was the impact of Reaganomics on labour rights?
p1: Deregulation and tax cuts for business — union-busting became standard practice. Employers used legal challenges, outsourcing and non-unionised temporary workers to weaken unions. Relocating to right-to-work states normalised.
p2: Reagan reduced OSHA funding — workplace safety declined, safety violations persisted especially in agriculture and construction. Judicial appointments shifted courts in a more employer-friendly direction — weakened NLRB enforcement.
p3: Union membership: 24% (1979) → 16% (1990). Manufacturing decline accelerated — 40% drop from 1970 peak by 1979 already embedded. Globalisation of production meant employers had leverage unions lacked — jobs could be outsourced rather than concessions made.

front: What was the right to strike and right to safe conditions like in 1865?
p1: Right to strike: fewer than 5% of strikes led to concessions 1865–75 — lack of solidarity and financial support. Scab labour widespread — in strikes of 100 workers, scabs typically comprised 20–30 replacements. Blacklisting shared among 50 mine operators in Pennsylvania. Courts issued injunctions against strikes in railroads — over 200,000 miles of track under private ownership by early 1870s.
p2: Molly Maguires (1873): violent conflicts in Pennsylvania coalfields between Irish labourers and mine owners. Pinkerton agents infiltrated — 10 leaders executed 1876. Associated unions with violence. Public hostility high — newspapers called strikers 'rioters' and 'anarchists'.
p3: Right to conditions: 3,000 railroad workers killed and 20,000 injured annually in early 1870s. Children as young as 8 worked 12-hour shifts for $1/week in cotton mills. No legal framework for benefits — injured workers left destitute. Contract system left workers vulnerable to layoffs during slow periods.

front: What was the impact of the Panic of 1873 and economic depression on labour?
p1: Panic of 1873: long economic depression — wages dropped by nearly half, widespread unemployment. 2% of population owned 30% of wealth. Unskilled workers earned only 30% of skilled workers' wages. Contract system left workers vulnerable — mass layoffs during slow periods.
p2: NLU collapsed — undermined by depression and internal divisions. Workers lacked financial reserves to sustain strikes — fewer than 5% of strikes led to concessions. Pattern repeated in late 1880s–90s: in 1892 alone the National Guard used 23 times to break strikes.
p3: Coxey's Army (1894): unemployed workers marched to Washington demanding federal job creation — failed to achieve aims. Exposed lack of federal sympathy for unemployed workers. Showed workers had no political leverage during downturns — government sided with employers during every economic crisis of the Gilded Age.

front: What was the role of racial and ethnic divisions in early industrialisation?
p1: Chinese Exclusion Act (1882): Chinese workers barred due to fears they undercut wages and weakened 'native' labour — passed with KOL support, exposing nativist bias even within inclusive-seeming unions. Immigrants 15–20% of urban industrial workforce — worked 60–70 hours/week for as little as $1/day.
p2: NLU excluded Black workers → CNLU formed separately (1869). African Americans used as strike-breakers — exacerbated mistrust between Black and white workers. Foran Act (1885): KOL pressure banned importing foreign labour under contract — first legislative gain against employer exploitation of division.
p3: Immigrant willingness to accept low wages angered native-born workers — employers deliberately encouraged division to undermine solidarity. Race to the bottom on wages made collective action harder. Division between workers a more fundamental obstacle than employer power alone.

front: How significant was opposition to advancements in labour rights during the New Deal?
p1: Employer resistance: many employers resisted Wagner Act through blacklisting, spy networks and private security. Henry Ford resisted UAW recognition until 1941. Memorial Day Massacre (1937): Chicago police killed 10 striking steelworkers — opposition was violent not just legal.
p2: Internal divisions: AFL-CIO split (1938) — AFL expelled CIO, exposing fractures. AFL promoted closed shops inadvertently excluding Black workers. NLRB v Fansteel (1939): sit-down strikes ruled illegal — legal opposition limited key tactic.
p3: Limits of opposition: union membership surged 3.7 million (1933) → 9 million (1938) despite resistance. US Steel unionised 1937 without a strike. Memorial Day Massacre backfired — public outrage strengthened solidarity. Wagner Act's legal framework ultimately overcame employer opposition.

front: What was the significance of the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire (1911)?
p1: 146 garment workers killed — mostly young immigrant women — due to locked exit doors, inadequate fire escapes and poor safety standards. Workers jumped from 8th floor to escape flames. Employer Isaac Harris and Max Blanck acquitted of manslaughter.
p2: Galvanised public demand for safety legislation — New York State Factory Investigating Commission established, leading to 30+ labour laws. Women's Trade Union League (WTUL, 1903) and International Ladies' Garment Workers' Union (ILGWU) gained members and political influence.
p3: Exposed the gap between industrial capitalism and worker protection — showed voluntary employer safety measures were insufficient. Became a defining moment for the progressive labour reform movement. Death toll highlighted particular vulnerability of immigrant women workers.

front: What was the significance of the Clayton Antitrust Act (1914)?
p1: Attempted to exempt unions from antitrust laws — amended Sherman Act by preventing courts using injunctions against strikes, boycotts and peaceful picketing. Declared that 'the labour of a human being is not a commodity.' Gompers called it 'labour's Magna Carta'.
p2: Impact limited: Duplex Printing Press v Deering (1921) — Supreme Court upheld use of injunctions against unions despite Clayton Act. Courts continued to treat secondary boycotts as illegal. Coppage v Kansas (1915): upheld yellow-dog contracts.
p3: Contrast: Norris-LaGuardia Act (1932) finally prohibited federal courts from issuing injunctions against peaceful strikes and made yellow-dog contracts unenforceable — achieved what Clayton Act had attempted. Together these show the long arc of legal struggle over the right to strike.

front: What was the significance of the Women's Trade Union League (1903)?
p1: Coalition of working-class women and middle-class reformers — advocated for better wages, shorter hours and unionisation for women workers. Actively supported Lawrence Textile Strike (1912) — helped women receive 15% pay rise and overtime pay.
p2: Exposed the exclusion of women from male-dominated unions like the AFL. Pushed for protective legislation for women workers — contributed to pressure that led to Keating-Owen Child Labour Act (1916) and later FLSA (1938).
p3: Limitations: AFL remained hostile to women's full membership. Triangle Shirtwaist Fire (1911) exposed inadequacy of existing protections. WTUL showed that middle-class advocacy was needed because working-class women lacked the political leverage to reform conditions alone.

front: What was the significance of the NIRA/NRA (1933) and why did it fail?
p1: National Industrial Recovery Act (1933): encouraged employers to adopt codes protecting workers — set minimum wages, maximum hours and recognised right to collective bargaining under Section 7a. Seen as precursor to Wagner Act. NRA Blue Eagle symbol displayed by compliant businesses.
p2: Declared unconstitutional by Supreme Court 1935 (Schechter Poultry v US) — exceeded federal power. Many employers displayed Blue Eagle without actually complying with its provisions. NRA codes often undermined by employers and manipulated to their advantage.
p3: Significance: NIRA's failure showed that voluntary codes were insufficient — accelerated pressure for mandatory enforcement through Wagner Act (1935). Section 7a had encouraged union organising — membership grew even before Wagner Act. Employer evasion demonstrated need for NLRB.

front: What was employer and state resistance to the New Deal labour reforms?
p1: Many employers actively resisted Wagner Act — blacklisting, spy networks and private security continued despite NLRB. Henry Ford: resisted UAW recognition until 1941 — one of last major industrial employers to accept union power. Textile Workers' Strike (1934): 400,000 workers — crushed with violence and repression.
p2: Memorial Day Massacre (1937): Chicago police killed 10 striking steelworkers at Republic Steel — employers used local and state authorities as instruments of suppression. Public outrage over incident strengthened union solidarity and embarrassed opponents of Wagner Act.
p3: Southern resistance: Southern Democrats maintained workplace segregation and racial hierarchies — Black workers excluded from unions, violent repression if they organised. Failure of New Deal to address workplace segregation allowed Southern employers to undermine gains. Some NRA codes contained racial wage differentials.

front: What was the significance of NLRB v Fansteel (1939) and Ford's recognition of the UAW (1941)?
p1: NLRB v Fansteel (1939): Supreme Court ruled sit-down strikes were an illegal form of labour dispute — undermined key CIO tactic that had won Flint (1936-7). Workers could be dismissed for occupying factories even if employer had violated Wagner Act.
p2: Ford recognition (1941): Henry Ford — last major industrial employer to accept union power — recognised UAW after NLRB election. Ford had used private security force (Service Department) to violently suppress organising — Battle of the Overpass (1937) saw UAW organisers beaten.
p3: Together these show the limits and possibilities of the New Deal framework: sit-down strikes outlawed but NLRB elections provided alternative route to recognition. Union membership continued to grow despite legal setbacks — 9 million by 1938, 14.8 million by 1945.

front: What was the post-WWII strike wave (1946) and its consequences?
p1: 1946: 5,000 strikes involving 4.6 million workers — largest strike wave in US history. Pent-up pressure after wartime no-strike pledges. Steel, auto, coal and electrical workers all struck. Truman seized steel mills and threatened to draft striking rail workers into the army.
p2: Public backlash: widespread disruption of essential services eroded public sympathy for unions. Republicans gained Congress in 1946 midterms — directly enabled Taft-Hartley Act (1947). Strike wave shown as evidence unions had too much power.
p3: Taft-Hartley (1947): passed over Truman's veto — banned secondary strikes and closed shops, allowed right-to-work laws (21 states), imposed 60-day cooling-off period, required anti-communist oaths. Post-war strike wave thus produced the most significant legislative rollback of union rights since before the New Deal.

front: What was the significance of the Landrum-Griffin Act (1959) and Kennedy EO 10988 (1962)?
p1: Landrum-Griffin Act (1959): increased federal oversight of union internal affairs — required regular elections, financial reporting and democratic procedures. Curtailed secondary boycotts and picketing further. Response to corruption in Teamsters and other unions revealed by Senate committee.
p2: Kennedy EO 10988 (1962): granted federal employees right to organise and collectively bargain — but not to strike. First significant extension of union rights to public sector. Led to rapid growth of public sector unions — American Federation of Government Employees.
p3: Together these represent the contradictions of the 1960s for labour: Landrum-Griffin curtailed union political activities while EO 10988 opened a new frontier. Public sector unionisation became the fastest-growing area of labour organisation — partially offsetting decline in manufacturing unions.

front: What was the impact of the Equal Pay Act (1963) and Civil Rights Act (1964) on labour rights?
p1: Equal Pay Act (1963): first federal law prohibiting pay discrimination based on sex — required equal pay for equal work in the same establishment. Limited in scope: applied only where work was substantially equal, allowed differentials based on seniority, merit or production.
p2: Civil Rights Act (1964) Title VII: prohibited employment discrimination by race, colour, religion, sex or national origin — established Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) to enforce. First time federal law comprehensively addressed workplace racial discrimination.
p3: Impact: by 1965 AFL-CIO members earned 20% more than non-unionised workers — but racial and gender pay gaps persisted. EEOC initially under-resourced. Women and minorities still disproportionately in lower-paid non-unionised roles. By 1990, service sector (70% of workforce) had weak union presence.

front: What was the significance of OSHA (1970)?
p1: Occupational Safety and Health Act (1970): established OSHA — first comprehensive federal workplace safety standards. Required employers to provide safe working conditions free from recognised hazards. Established right to refuse unsafe work and report violations without retaliation.
p2: Impact: by 1990s workplace fatalities decreased to approximately 4,500 annually from over 14,000 in the 1930s. Significant improvement in dangerous industries — mining, construction, manufacturing. Product of union-led campaigns and broader progressive political coalition.
p3: Limits: Reagan reduced OSHA funding — safety violations persisted especially in agriculture and construction. Non-unionised sectors particularly vulnerable — immigrant workers in agriculture and service industries faced worst conditions with limited enforcement. By 1992, service sector (70% of workforce) had weak OSHA coverage.

front: What was the significance of Red Cloud's War (1866–68) and the Treaty of Fort Laramie?
p1: Red Cloud's War (1866–8): Sioux led by Red Cloud successfully forced U.S. Army to abandon Bozeman Trail forts — one of the few Native American military victories that led to a favourable treaty. Treaty of Fort Laramie (1868): recognised Sioux control of Black Hills and the Great Sioux Reservation.
p2: Treaty also confined Sioux to increasingly smaller areas — beginning of reservation system. Victory short-lived: gold discovered in Black Hills (1874) — government attempted to buy land, Sioux refused. 1877: government seized Black Hills in direct violation of Fort Laramie Treaty — threatened to starve Sioux unless they gave up the land.
p3: Significance: showed that military resistance could force federal concessions — but federal government would violate treaties when economic interests demanded. US v Sioux Nation (1980): Supreme Court eventually ruled seizure illegal, awarded $106 million — Sioux refused, demanded land returned.

front: What was the significance of the Sand Creek Massacre (1864) and buffalo extermination?
p1: Sand Creek Massacre (1864): Colorado militia attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho village — killed over 150 men, women and children under a white flag of truce. Commander Colonel Chivington faced no criminal charges. Demonstrated that militia violence against peaceful Natives went unpunished.
p2: Buffalo extermination: U.S. Army deliberately killed an estimated 10 million buffalo 1865–83 — direct attack on Plains tribes' food, clothing, shelter and spiritual practices. Federal government encouraged hunting to force Natives onto reservations. Buffalo population fell from 30 million (1860) to less than 1,000 (1889).
p3: Combined impact: land loss through violence + destruction of food source = forced dependency on government rations. Plains tribes had no economic alternative to reservation life. Deliberately engineered conditions of poverty and dependency that persisted throughout the period.

front: What was the significance of the Battle of Little Bighorn (1876)?
p1: Lakota Sioux and Cheyenne forces led by Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated General Custer and killed 200 men — one of the most significant Native military victories of the era. Showed Plains tribes could defeat U.S. military when united and well-led.
p2: BUT prompted harsh federal response — government intensified military campaigns, seized Black Hills (1877) in violation of Fort Laramie Treaty. By end of 1870s all Plains tribes confined to reservations. Battle of Little Bighorn inspired rather than deterred federal dispossession.
p3: Broader significance: led some Americans to question federal policy — Helen Hunt Jackson's 'A Century of Dishonour' (1881) exposed U.S. mistreatment of Native Americans partly in response. Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse became symbols of Native resistance. Ultimate failure showed limits of military resistance alone without broader political change.

front: What was the impact of the Homestead Act (1862) and transcontinental railroad on Native Americans?
p1: Homestead Act (1862): granted settlers 160-acre plots in the West — directly encroached on Native lands already established by treaty. Opened floodgates to settler expansion onto Plains previously acknowledged as Native territory.
p2: Transcontinental railroad completed (1869): opened West to settlers, miners and cattle ranchers. Government granted railway companies land taken from tribes — railroad companies received alternating sections of land up to 20 miles either side of track. Destroyed buffalo migration patterns, enabling mass slaughter.
p3: Indian Appropriations Act (1871): ended treaty-making — tribes no longer recognised as independent nations. Combination of Homestead Act, railroad and end of treaties removed all legal protections for Native land. By 1870, over 30,000 troops stationed across West to enforce this dispossession.

front: What was the Dawes Severalty Act (1887) and how did it work?
p1: Dawes Act (1887): divided communal tribal lands into individual 160-acre allotments (320 acres for grazing) per male head of family — directly imposed Western individual land ownership onto communal Native cultures. 'Surplus' land after allotment sold to white settlers.
p2: Native landowners who accepted allotments became taxpayers and gained rights of citizenship after 25 years — federal government framed this as uplift. Five Civilised Tribes (Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Creek, Seminole) initially exempt until Curtis Act (1898) extended it to them.
p3: Mechanism of dispossession: Native land fell from 156 million acres (1881) to 78 million acres by 1890 — lost 78 million acres in three years. By 1934 total had fallen to 48 million acres. Dead Indian Act (1902): allowed sale of inherited land, accelerating further loss. Designed to destroy communal basis of tribal life.

front: What was the cultural and gendered impact of the Dawes Act?
p1: Imposed male-headed family ownership onto matriarchal tribes — Iroquois and Cherokee women traditionally managed land and property. Dawes Act gave land to male heads of families, stripping women of economic power and undermining tribal governance structures rooted in women's authority.
p2: Disrupted communal landholding that formed the social and economic basis of tribal life. Allotment land often poor quality and sold to white speculators when Natives could not farm it — majority sold their land, leaving them destitute. Most failed to adapt to individual farming under allotment system.
p3: Cultural loss: broke up the spatial concentration of tribes — scattered families across allotments, undermining community gatherings, ceremonies and traditional governance. Combined with boarding schools and buffalo extermination = systematic destruction of the material and cultural basis of Native life.
